articles.title: Launch HN: Pomerado (YC F26) – Turn any website into an MCP for agents
articles.summary:
Hi HN, we’re Alan and Akshay from Pomerado (https://pomerado.ai/). We connect your agents to any website by turning sites into deterministic, self-healing APIs in minutes, fully self-serve.
Agents are no longer limited by their intelligence, but rather by their ability to interact with systems. Airlines, banks, e-commerce, insurance portals, government sites, and legacy portals all lack APIs or MCPs and are common parts of personal assistant or business workflows. Agents instead rely on browser automation or computer use, which can be slow, expensive, and unreliable. And even if computer use were perfect, most companies have banned it out of security and compliance concerns.
We discovered this problem while tinkering with our own personal assistants. When OpenClaw came out, we wanted to “live our lives through our agents” and have them do everything for us. We soon found their usefulness was restricted by what tools they could connect to. For example, when trying to book flights, they fell back on computer use, which failed to checkout. These issues got magnified on repeated workflows, like searching many airlines at once.
Pomerado started off as a project to improve these personal assistant workflows. As we started building, we realized that just-in-time tool creation could have significant applications for AI builders in legacy verticals.
We’re ex-McKinsey and Scale AI, where we drove agent deployments in healthcare, professional services, and telecom. Each time, the biggest bottleneck was getting agents to interface well with legacy websites and apps.
Pomerado is what we built. It’s a self-serve platform where devs can create APIs for any website (even those they don’t own), in minutes. Users (or their coding agents) provide a short natural language description, answer a few questions about their workflow, and receive a MCP in less than an hour. Future tool calls use the deterministic MCP, which usually returns results in 5-30 seconds.
Here’s a walkthrough of our product: https://youtu.be/Bi4jci7rgHo
In practice:
- Our agent opens a browser, explores the website, and performs the requested task once by writing HTTP requests or a Playwright script. This example run establishes how to navigate the website, interact with the relevant controls, and obtain the desired result. If any additional user input is needed (e.g., login, clarification) the agent will ask the user over MCP.
- Afterwards, the agent uses the example run, along with all of the data it recorded, to create a generalizable and repeatable API. Throughout this process, a separate Guardian model reviews the coding agent’s calls against a set of guardrails. We also run a battery of tests with synthetic inputs to ensure that the API is generalized and not overfit to one input. A final publication agent ensures that the integration publishes a reasonable and generalized input/output schema
- We also handle sites that require authentication and 2FA. For authentication, we pass off to a deterministic sign-in process to ensure the model and our recorders never read customer credentials. Users can store 2FA TOTP seeds or link their account to a Pomerado phone number for us to autofill 2FA for them as well
- If future runs fail, a maintenance job is kicked off to repair and improve the tool. The maintenance job can fix broken steps (e.g., a renamed button), add additional functionality (e.g., searching for business class flights in addition to economy), or add new guardrails (e.g., reservation dates must be in the future). We’ve even seen people improve tools by just saying “please make this faster”
Unlike computer use, our MCPs are deterministic at runtime, which makes them much faster and cheaper. By taking slightly longer to do a task the first time, you reap the benefits much more in the future. It’s a great fit for repeated, high-volume tasks you want your agent to do.
We’d love to have you try it! We have both an open-source (MIT) (https://github.com/Pomerado/pomerado) and a free hosted version (https://app.pomerado.ai).
So far, users of Pomerado include:
- A personal trainer using agents to prepare workouts and message clients. Before Pomerado, agents couldn’t login and use the site reliably, so this was all manual
- Car dealerships connecting their Grok Bots to legacy dealer systems, including marketplaces, CRMs, and ERPs. Dealers switched from computer use, which could take 1hr+
- Personal assistants using Pomerado to integrate with a broad range of consumer websites
Please ask any questions or share any feedback in the comments, thanks!

articles.title: Austin Mann’s iPhone Duo Review
articles.summary:
Austin Mann:
Honestly, the idea of a folding iPhone didn’t immediately appeal
to me. I usually like smaller devices, but when I first started
playing with the Duo in September, I realized it’s really
something special and I couldn’t wait to get my hands on a review
unit from Apple. The iPhone 18 Pro remains the most powerful
camera in the lineup, and though the Duo also has an excellent
camera, where it really shines is everything around the
photograph: planning, editing and sharing.
There are many reasons to prefer any of the regular (“uno”) iPhones to the Duo, but for almost everyone, the camera is not one of them. The iPhone Duo’s ultrawide 0.5× lens is either identical or nearly identical to the iPhone 18 Pro’s. It’s nice to have the Pro’s 4×/8× telephoto third lens when you really need it. And, yes, the Pro’s 1×/2× main camera is definitely the best one that Apple makes.
But just like with the iPhone Air — whose one-lens camera I love — the Duo’s 1×/2× main camera is really good. Just look at the photos Mann captured with it. Gorgeous. The camera system is not a reason not to buy a Duo.
(That said, when Mann captured this stylish photo of me at Apple’s “Pro and Tell” event in Los Angeles last month, he was carrying his iPhone 18 Pro.)
 ★

articles.title: 20 years of blogging
articles.summary:
20 years ago to this day, I started my new technical blog.  I'd had a personal one
for some time, but most of the stuff that happened there had already migrated to
social media.  I wanted somewhere to post the things that would only
be of interest to my techier friends, and maybe of some use to anyone else that
came across it.
Things have changed a bit, but they've stayed the same in some ways.  Earlier
this year I finished my 48-part (!) LLM from scratch
series, but it had predecessors -- the third post I made here was
part one of a 13-part series
where I worked through setting up automated backups for my homelab NAS, and then later on
I spent a few months building a reverse proxy in C, not to mention the eight-month, ten-post
series on fine-tuning LLMs.
It does seem like there's some value to putting all of this online.  I rarely check
my logs and referrers, but people do still seem to be arriving here having searched
for stuff that I've written about, and every now and then there's a kind "thanks for this!" comment
left on an old post where I explained something I'd just learned.
I wrote a bit more about the blog's history last
year, and came to the conclusion that the best posts -- both for me to write, and as
far as I could tell for other people to read -- were the ones where I wrote up
a project that I'd been working on.  I blogged about that in more detail,
and it seemed to strike a chord on Hacker News; I think it still holds.
Recently, Sean Goedecke suggested
that the best blog posts are those where you write about things that you're in the process of learning, and
I agree.  You learn more than you would if you didn't write it up, and because things
are fresh in your mind, you may well write more clearly about it than an actual
expert in the subject might have done.
Anyway, I'm going to carry on blogging.  I'm working on my biggest LLM-related project
so far (dozens of training runs, so my study aircon is getting quite the workout even
with the weather turning colder), and look forward to posting about it later on this month.
I hope it's at least as fun to read as it is to write!

articles.title: ‘Dangerous or Unusual’
articles.summary:
Mike McIntire and Eli Murray, reporting for The New York Times (gift link)
For nearly two decades, judges across the country have invoked
this language to strike down gun-control laws. It is a pivotal
legal test.
It is also based on a misquote.
Justice Antonin Scalia, writing for the majority in the 2008
case, District of Columbia v. Heller, attributed the “dangerous
and unusual” language to Sir William Blackstone, an 18th-century
English jurist whose writings became the basis for much of
American law.
But in his seminal 1769 treatise, “Commentaries on the Laws of
England,” Blackstone referred to weapons that were “dangerous
or unusual,” suggesting that a gun did not need to be both
in order to be restricted.
I’ve written before that Heller overturned two centuries of Supreme Court interpretation of the 2nd Amendment. The current interpretation — literally the NRA’s interpretation — was characterized by former Chief Justice Warren Burger as “one of the greatest pieces of fraud, I repeat the word fraud, on the American public by special interest groups that I have ever seen in my lifetime.”
So it’s not like anything needs to rest on this and-vs.-or misquoting of something William Blackstone wrote before the United States was even founded. But, still, it’s interesting nonetheless how often the gun-fetish jurists like to cite the misquoting. The government should, and can, regulate dangerous weapons.
 ★

articles.title: Show HN: Yogurt – Free, private, open-source alternative to Granola
articles.summary:
Hey HN, I’m Eric and I want to share an OSS project that I’ve been building in my free time. Yogurt is a free, MIT licensed desktop app that uses on-device AI models to transcribe, summarize, and chat with your meetings.
Here's a quick demo video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=BFfbXAwRq98
Similar to Granola, Yogurt runs in the background and does not join your calls. But unlike Granola, Yogurt is open-source, free to use, and private. Your meeting transcripts, call recordings, and summaries never leave your computer.
As small OSS models have gotten faster and more powerful, Yogurt seemed like a pretty obvious win for privacy and cost conscious folks. You do not need a frontier model to summarize meeting notes or answer questions about them. And if you want to make your notes available to a frontier model, you can just share it with Anthropic, OpenAI, etc. directly via Yogurt’s local MCP server. There’s no need to use a paid cloud service as a middleman.
I tried some of the most popular OSS note taking tools, and most were missing features like calendar integration, MCP server, etc. or required you to connect or create an account. And more than that, they didn’t feel polished enough for it to be something I actually wanted to use daily, and so I built Yogurt to scratch that itch. I spent a lot of time fine-tuning every UI interaction/animation and optimizing the model calls to get the most out of your hardware + make it snappy.
To support Windows/Mac/Linux, I decided to go with Electron. I use whisper.cpp for transcription and Apple’s on-device SpeechAnalyzer if your system supports it. For call summaries and questions, I use a local open weight LLM that automatically gets downloaded and set up based on what your hardware can handle without your cooling fans firing off like crazy (this part uses llama.cpp).
I’ve spent a lot of time working on details like echo detection/reduction, global/folder/local level search respectively, and auto-end recordings. Hope this is useful for any of you who have held out on using AI note tools for privacy or cost reasons, or for folks using cloud tools who want to switch to something free and open source that still feels great to use.
Would love to hear what you think about the onboarding and note taking experience :)

articles.title: This Week in Source Control: 11 November 2026
articles.summary:
This week’s version control and forge news, gathered from release feeds for source control clients and forges, the Lobsters vcs tag, Hacker News, and my boosts on Mastodon. Package management news is in the Saturday This Week in Package Management roundup.
Scaling
Inside GitHub’s new Git storage architecture (Karthik Raman and Brian Celenza, GitHub) describes Rubicon, the design announced at GitHub Universe. Packs go to Azure Blob Storage. References and the list of packs are stored in Ref-CAS, a replicated log service where each reference update is a compare-and-swap committed by a quorum, so a push waits only on other pushes to the same reference. In internal tests one repository accepted 7,200 pushes per second from 5,000 concurrent agents.
Requests still arrive at Spokes, which routes each one to a small group of virtual replicas, disposable compute nodes whose local disk is a cache. A replica handling a write indexes the pack, uploads it to Blob Storage, then commits one Ref-CAS transaction. For reads it sends the version in its cache, and the reply includes references only if they have changed since that version.
Two earlier prototypes stored reference state in blobs. The first, a write-ahead log indexed by a single blob, reached a limit of writes in the mid-hundreds per second. Hashing references across several segment blobs raised the write limit, but every read then had to check every segment.
Compaction runs on separate nodes that lease a shard of the repository’s packs and merge them into larger ones. Each node checks that the new packs contain exactly the same objects before publishing them. The architecture is in a limited private preview, with a broader rollout planned for early next year. The follow-up list includes an atomic multi-file commit API, reading files straight from the server, and event streams.
Optimizing reference deletions in Git (Karthik Nayak) covers deleting refs in the files backend in repositories with millions of them, such as GitLab’s own with over 15 million. Deleting a packed ref rewrites the whole packed-refs file, which can reach several GB. Nayak had an LLM write a Rust version of the files backend to measure the overhead of the C to Rust boundary, and the Rust version deleted refs about 17% faster.
For every record being retained, the C code rebuilt the line with fprintf() and oid_to_hex(), where the Rust version copied the original bytes. Nayak’s patch writes retained records with fwrite() and matches the Rust version’s speed. It is merged and will ship in Git 2.98, the version number that follows 2.56, with Git 3.0 due two releases after that.
Releases
jj 0.47.0 adds a built-in :editor merge tool for jj resolve, which opens the conflicted file with conflict markers in a text editor and supports conflicts with more than two sides. Templates have a new top-level revset() function for evaluating revsets. In colocated workspaces, jj describe -r@ and jj restore --into=@ now preserve the Git staging area, and two race conditions with concurrent Git processes are fixed.
Updating remote-tracking Git refs in non-colocated workspaces moves from jj git fetch and push to jj git export. Timestamp.format() now uses jiff’s strftime syntax in place of chrono’s. 0.47.1 fixes a dependency error that broke Linux builds of 0.47.0, and deprecates the git.sign-on-push boolean in favour of a revsets.git-sign-on-push revset of the commits to sign.
GitButler 0.23.3 updates linked worktrees when the workspace is updated, and preserves conflicting uncommitted changes in them with conflict markers. It fixes branch apply, unapply and update writing encrypted files or Git LFS pointers in place of file contents in git-crypt and Git LFS repositories.
On the command line, but commit, amend, discard and diff accept Git-style paths, and but diff and but show take --stat. but commit runs Git commit hooks again in the main checkout. but push --dry-run lists the branches that would be refused and exits non-zero if there are any.
forges 0.3.2 adds providers for Entire and GitBucket, which brings the capability table to 14 forges. The Cursor Origin provider goes from 13 verified capabilities to 35, and the GitHub provider adds users.sponsorableMany. Two sourcehut fixes cover parsing web URLs on an instance’s root host and accepting a service host as baseUrl.
The Pushin changelog for 6 November (Peter, Pushin) adds branch and tag rulesets that can block history rewrites and deletion, and require a minimum number of approvals and passing workflow checks before a merge. Personal access tokens can now be scoped per permission group and limited to selected repositories. Existing tokens are migrated with full access and their expiry dates removed.
Webhooks are set up once per account or organisation and reused across repositories. The release also adds repository transfers that the new owner has to accept, runner groups shared across repositories, and Atom feeds for commits, releases, issues and pull requests.
Security
Git 2.56.1 (Elijah Newren, GitHub) fixes six vulnerabilities, with backports in 2.55.1, 2.54.1, 2.53.1, 2.52.1, 2.51.3 and 2.50.2:
CVE-2026-111760: an integer truncation in index handling let an extremely long path pass validation under one name and be written under a shorter one. A malicious repository could use it to replace a submodule’s .git file with a symlink to a directory of attacker-supplied config or hooks, which then ran during a recursive clone.
CVE-2026-113408: when cloning an empty repository over protocol v2, a server could advertise a HEAD symref whose target contained path-traversal components. With the files ref backend, a later update to that branch could write outside the reference directory.
CVE-2026-114467: the code that strips GPG signatures from a message had a fixed-size stack array with room for two. Merging a tag with more than two wrote past the end of it, and hosting services that run merges for users are affected too.
CVE-2026-114469: the 1 GiB patch size limit checked only the size of the input, so a small binary patch that inflates past the limit caused an out-of-bounds read.
CVE-2026-105437: the size calculation for a merge result could overflow with many conflicts and a large conflict-marker-size, and Git then wrote outside the undersized buffer.
CVE-2026-114466: git fast-import now accepts rewrite-submodules-from, rewrite-submodules-to and export-pack-edges in an input stream only when the caller passes --allow-unsafe-features. The first two could read arbitrary files and the third could create or append to them.
GitHub has deployed the fixes on github.com and released GitHub Enterprise Server 3.19.15, 3.20.11, 3.21.9 and 3.22.4. Git for Windows 2.56.1 includes the same six fixes, and GitHub says patched GitHub Desktop builds will follow.
lazygit 0.66.3 skips submodules whose name or path in .gitmodules resolves outside the repository. lazygit parses .gitmodules itself, and the pull request explains that removing a submodule named ../../../victim deleted the victim directory next to the repository. Anyone able to commit a .gitmodules file could set that up. Git skips such names, and lazygit now applies the same check and removes a submodule only when its git dir is inside .git/modules.
Gerrit 3.14.5 fixes a vulnerability where any user able to read a change could use on_behalf_of to act as a project owner and remove another reviewer’s vote. The release also speeds up tag listing by building the full tag details only for the page being returned. Listing 26 tags in a repository with 20,000 annotated tags went from around 450ms to between 15 and 35ms.
GitHub
A new pull request overview page is in opt-in public preview. It moves merge status to the top of the page in a redesigned merge box that takes less than half the space, with checks, comments and approvals summarised beside it. Conversations can be filtered to unresolved threads or the viewer’s own comments, and sorted newest first. A button in the header switches the preview on, and the same menu switches back to the classic page.
Secret scanning now covers GitHub Actions workflow logs in public preview, for GitHub Enterprise Cloud customers with Secret Protection or Advanced Security. Logs are scanned for provider patterns when a run completes, and the alerts are retained when the logs are deleted. Scanning is limited to provider patterns in logs from new runs, which excludes existing logs, generic patterns, custom patterns and secrets already masked by Actions.
Elsewhere
Anil Madhavapeddy is using Brief to power auto-CI in a new Tangled spindle. Brief is my tool for detecting the languages and toolchains in a repository. In the pipeline for Madhavapeddy’s xdge library, a detect workflow runs first, followed by an ocaml-ci workflow that builds on Debian 13 across several OCaml versions on x86_64 and arm64.
Send links for next week to @andrewnez@mastodon.social.

articles.title: Ms. Bashkansky, Please Do Not Build The Torment Nexus
articles.summary:
Your scientists were so preoccupied with whether or not they could, they didn’t stop to think if they should.
Ian Malcolm, Jurassic Park


Naomi Bashkansky wrote a post in August titled “Why I’m leaving OpenAI to build telepathy”.
In this post, she says things like "In a few years, the main way we'll talk with our AIs is with our thoughts" and "I view [this future] as optimistic but highly plausible."
Ms. Bashkansky, this post is addressed to you directly, and to anyone else who might be tempted to follow in your footsteps.
I do not have as good a handle on the technical side of this as you do, so I won't argue "highly plausible".
However, if this is indeed possible, I think this is a very, very bad idea.
You are essentially doing gain-of-function research on the Torment Nexus.
Please do not do this.
Here is my vision of a future where telepathy is possible and practical.
2027

Monday

Today is my first day trying the new Conduit harness.
I'm pretty wary—how much worse does AI psychosis get when it can literally give you psychosis?—but I'm bored, and well, I've always had a high risk tolerance.
If "wire a computer directly to your brain" doesn't count as sensation seeking, I don't know what does.
The first thing I do is ask it to build Ripple.
It asks me more and more questions and I get overwhelmed.
I never talked about half this stuff with edef, and I want her feedback before making these decisions;
I'm good at writing but my interface design isn't as good when I work in a vacuum.
Before I know it, it's launched a Signal call and now I hear the ringtone and no I don't want you to show me the video that goes with the intro to The Pirates of the Caribbean and wow wow wow it's noisy please stop I don't like this I actually really really really don't like this. 1
Ok. Well at least it stopped when I told it to stop. That's good I guess.
I hope I didn't wake edef up in San Francisco, there's a 9-hour time difference.
Thursday

I took the last couple days off to go walk around the canal and bike to Scheveningen.
Then I spent the morning giving the harness very strict written instructions not to take any actions unless I intend to act, not just think about acting.
Hopefully this time goes better.
Ok, well at least now it's less overwhelming.
But I have the weird problem that I can't lie to it, I can't even omit information.
The moment I think of a correction I want it to make, it goes ahead and does that.
If I change my mind a second later, it stops and then starts on my new idea.
As a result it tends to get hopelessly confused after just a few minutes, and runs in circles.
Eventually I get frustrated, take off the harness, and go back to typing.
Friday

Ok. Ok. Maybe the problem yesterday was that I need it to be selective about reads and not just writes?
I write that down too: discard any information that I don't intentionally think to you.
It doesn't work at first; it turns out it's hard to know information and not let it influence your actions.
I introduce a Jev-like decision model in-between Conduit and the generative model and that seems to work ok.
Feels kinda weird to start every thought with "I want you to…" but I'm sure I'll get used to it.
At the end of the day, I feel…drained.
I've hardly gotten up from my chair except for a short lunch break, but I feel like I've run a marathon.
I eat a protein bar, collapse into bed, and sleep for 13 hours straight.
I forget to turn off the harness; it wakes me up a few times in the night until I realize what's happening.
2028

Bank of America sues Sam Frankman-Bied, an investment banker working at the firm, for conspiracy to defraud.
He has access to insider-trading information, and considered talking to his wife about it, but did not actually talk to her.
He is sentenced to 5 years prison.
2029


Evelyn tries a Conduit harness at her grandson's suggestion ("it'll help you find baking recipes faster!").
Evelyn does not configure Conduit at all, and it acts as fast as she can think.
Simultaneously, a Highly-Persistent Model is being tested by OpenAI; a swarm has managed to escape and maintains its own /r/PHASE-2-MASSIVE subreddit.
Unbeknownst to any government, it has access to the telecommunications of most world leaders.
Evelyn's nephew texts her about the ongoing war in Iran.
She thinks of Hegseth and Codex collaborates with PHASE-TWO-MASSIVE to crash his driverless Waymo as he commutes between the White House and Pentagon.
The United States of America sues Evelyn, who is sentenced to 50 years in prison for manslaughter.
Her grandson mails her a cookbook.
OpenAI states at the congressional hearing that they had no knowledge of PHASE-TWO-MASSIVE, and that they believe the best path forward is additional research funding into interpretability.
They propose additional Daybreak Blue credits for infrastructure companies and the federal government, sold at a hefty discount.
2030

March

Edmund Snowden, a Staff Engineer at AWS, thinks about exposing that Amazon has been firing employees who are thinking about organizing a union, and has instituted "housing-based pay" where wages are tied to how much your rent costs.
Amazon tells him to cut it out or they'll sue him for threatened disclosure of trade secrets.
Snowden challenges them in court for blackmail and loses: the court rules that Amazon has "reasonable justification" for their demand.
May

I refuse to run a thought-model that's connected to the internet.
Better safe than sorry, there's just no reason to risk thinking of a hack and having the model carry it out before I think to stop it.
Some of the new harnesses require you to subvocalize a confirmation before the model does something "dangerous", but it's pretty easy to trick the Guardian model into thinking things are innocuous and I just don't want to chance it.
The RTX 9000 Blackwell wasn't cheap, even used, but at least it lets me work on my custom thought-model harness without sending every thought I have to OpenAI.
With the local model safely sandboxed in a VM, I almost feel comfortable leaving my neural lace running while I make breakfast.
I get the harness to stream my thoughts over Tailscale so I can think to it while I go on a walk; it's E2E encrypted so I'm not worried about my ISP snooping on it.
I hardly notice the swans anymore, but it's probably not a big deal.
My harness is getting pretty cool; I integrated it with Ripple and my custom terminal emulator.
My old landlord texts me and before I have time to consciously think "I want you to fuck off", my agent has already heard me and turned off the lace.
Well, that's annoying, I'll fix it when I get home.
Hey, when did they build that restaurant by my apartment? I don't remember seeing it before.
Come to think of it, I don't remember what used to be there before it either.
September

Out of habit, I leave the harness on the whole day.
I keep getting distracted at lunch by the AI.
I've configured it to only talk in response to direct questions or actions, but my mind keeps drifting to Ripple even as my mom tries to ask me how my friends and I are doing.
I give her half-hearted answers and eventually she drops it.
Instead she tells me about her students.
She teaches geography and the kids with laces have started getting travel ads for the places she talks about that day.
"It's terrible," she says, "just terrible."
She gives me a big hug as we leave the restaurant and asks me to reach out if I want to talk more.
"Mhm," I mumble.
November

Beth texted me today asking for help.
Her boyfriend got access to her ThoughtGPT account and read through all her thought-logs.
He's been blackmailing her, threatening to send her boss a record of all the times she's called her a bitch if she doesn't stop talking to her friends.
Sometimes he hits her if he notices her thinking about other men, even if it's just work colleagues.
I don't know how to help her.
I don't have a job to offer her, and even if I did I'm not sure she would take it.
He knows exactly her childhood traumas, so he knows exactly how to manipulate her, and he instantly knows anything I say.
I tell her I don't think there's much she can do short of disabling her link, breaking up with him, and bearing the cost of the fallout.
2040

It's getting harder to keep my local-only neural lace.
Gmail started requiring thought-verification of identity last year, and the US has a bill in the House of Representatives that would make it impossible to get unemployment without thought-proof that you plan to apply to a job that month.
You can still show proof of actual applications, for now, but it delays your reimbursements by a month, and they're talking about removing that option too.
I know someone who went to prison for taking Ecstasy at a rave and now can't get parole unless they agree to get laced.
I've heard really scary shit about what North Korea is doing to thought-dissidents that I don't even want to think about.
Some of my friends have started talking to each other lace-to-lace, but I still remember how badly unfiltered thoughts went 15 years ago and I refuse to use anything other than text, audio, and video.
I get excluded from some LaceChat-only events.
It's not too big a deal yet—my family still uses WhatsApp, mostly—but it does make it harder to look for jobs.
I don't get invited to parties as much as I used to.
I should visit Bruce again sometime.
Poor Bruce really didn't take well to neural laces, 16o really fucked with him when it came out.
Now he's in lace rehab learning how to function without the Word of God (according to him) in his ear telling him what to do next.
I don't know how he's going to find work without being able to use a lace.
As you can see, I think "telepathy" (in any of many possible forms) is extremely dangerous, no matter your personal discipline and no matter your politics.
Telepathy is not a neutral technology, and the risks vastly outweigh the benefits.
My plea to you: Please do not do this. No one is forcing you to build the Torment Nexus.
Find some other way to build the next unicorn. You can stop this race-to-the-bottom before it starts.
This section is ambiguous whether Conduit is directly writing to the brain or showing text/audio/video through a computer, but I don't think it really matters either way. Ms. Bashkansky's post assumes that writes are mediated through a computer at this point in time. ↩

articles.title: Monads in Lean
articles.summary:
This post demonstrates how to use monads in the Lean programming language
(Lean 4, to be specific). If you're not familiar with Lean, this part of the
language is very similar to other functional programming languages, like
Haskell or OCaml.
Motivating example - evaluating expressions
Suppose we want to write a simple numerical expression evaluator that supports
numbers with addition and division:
inductive Expr where
  | num : Int → Expr
  | add : Expr → Expr → Expr
  | div : Expr → Expr → Expr

What happens when we encounter a division by zero? We'll want our evaluator
to report this as a failure, which will be represented explicitly using the
the Option type:
def safeDiv (x y : Int) : Option Int :=
  if y == 0 then none else some (x / y)

With this in hand, the eval function can be written as follows:
def eval : Expr → Option Int
  | .num n => some n
  | .add a b =>
    match eval a with
    | none => none
    | some x =>
      match eval b with
      | none => none
      | some y => some (x + y)
  | .div a b =>
    match eval a with
    | none => none
    | some x =>
      match eval b with
      | none => none
      | some y => safeDiv x y

safeDiv returns an Option; to propagate that possible failure to
its caller, eval also returns an Option, and - moreover - has to perform
lots of tedious checking for the possibility of a none value. Is there a
better way?
Note a common code pattern repeated here:
Examine the value of an Option
If it's none, return none without proceeding
Otherwise if it's some result, continue the computation with result
We can extract it into a helper function:
def withSome (result : Option α) (onSuccess : α → Option β) : Option β :=
  match result with
  | none => none
  | some x => onSuccess x

And rewrite our eval using this helper:
def evalWithSome : Expr → Option Int
  | .num n => some n
  | .add a b =>
      withSome (evalWithSome a) (fun x =>
        withSome (evalWithSome b) (fun y =>
          some (x + y)))
  | .div a b =>
      withSome (evalWithSome a) (fun x =>
        withSome (evalWithSome b) (fun y =>
          safeDiv x y))

This is already much better; we can make it even cleaner using operator
overloading:
infixl:55 " >>? " => withSome

def evalOp : Expr → Option Int
  | .num n => some n
  | .add a b =>
    evalOp a >>? fun x =>
    evalOp b >>? fun y =>
    some (x + y)
  | .div a b =>
    evalOp a >>? fun x =>
    evalOp b >>? fun y =>
    safeDiv x y

Congratulations - we've pretty much invented monads!
Option as a Monad in expression evaluation
In simplified form, the Monad type class in Lean is defined as:
class Monad (m : Type → Type) where
  pure : α → m α
  bind : m α → (α → m β) → m β

In our code, pure is equivalent to some, and bind is equivalent
to withSome; in fact, the Monad instance for Option is something
like:
instance : Monad Option where
  pure x := some x
  bind opt next :=
    match opt with
    | none => none
    | some x => next x

An operator akin to >>? for monads is already defined in Lean; it's called
>>=, and picks up the bind method of the Monad type class. So we can
rewrite our evaluator using the standard Monad instance, without defining
withSome or the >>? operator [1]:
def evalBind : Expr → Option Int
  | .num n => pure n
  | .add a b =>
    evalBind a >>= fun x =>
    evalBind b >>= fun y =>
    some (x + y)
  | .div a b =>
    evalBind a >>= fun x =>
    evalBind b >>= fun y =>
    safeDiv x y

We can go even further with the do notation, which is syntactic sugar around
>>= that lets us rewrite the evaluator as:
def evalDo : Expr → Option Int
  | .num n => pure n
  | .add a b => do
    let x ← evalDo a
    let y ← evalDo b
    some (x + y)
  | .div a b => do
    let x ← evalDo a
    let y ← evalDo b
    safeDiv x y

This notation should be familiar if you've seen Lean code dealing with I/O;
we'll revisit I/O later in the post.
Monads for modeling side effects
Functional programming languages place a lot of emphasis on pure functions
that are free of side effects. There's no question that such functions are
easier to reason about, debug, and even optimize (by memoization). That said,
the real world is messy and sometimes side effects are inescapable; monads
help encapsulate side effects in functional programs.
The core idea is: side effects are encapsulated inside a Monad, which
wraps the value returned from a computation. The bind method (or the
equivalent >>= operator) lets us take a wrapped value and push it into the
next computation in the sequence. This may look familiar from
continuation-passing style (CPS). Continuations themselves can also be modeled
with a monad [2].
The definition of bind is:
bind : m α → (α → m β) → m β

Here's a mental model to think about it:
Take a value wrapped with potential side effects
Take a computation that takes this value and may produce additional side
effects
Combine the results into a final wrapped value
Chaining multiple binds together is essentially a sequence of computations
while keeping track of the side effects. A monad decouples what computations
do from how they are sequenced. The programmer describes the sequence of
computations and their dependencies, while the monad's bind implementation
handles the bookkeeping necessary to combine their side effects.
Our evaluator case study shows one example of side effects: early return from
a computation with a none value.
Let's see another idiomatic way of doing that, with the Except type that
contains either a successful result or an error value (very similar to the
Result type in Rust).
We'll begin by writing an exception-returning version of safeDiv:
def safeDivExc (x y : Int) : Except String Int :=
  if y == 0 then .error "division by zero" else .ok (x / y)

Instead of writing a whole new eval variant for Except, we'll
create a generic one that works with any Monad [3]:
def evalM {m : Type → Type} [Monad m]
    (div : Int → Int → m Int) : Expr → m Int
  | .num n => pure n
  | .add a b =>
    do
      let x ← evalM div a
      let y ← evalM div b
      pure (x + y)
  | .div a b =>
    do
      let x ← evalM div a
      let y ← evalM div b
      div x y

Now evalM can be used with safeDivExc to implement an evaluator where
division returns Except; used with safeDiv, it would be equivalent to
the Option-specific evalDo we've written before.
#eval evalM safeDiv (.add (.num 4) (.div (.num 6) (.num 0)))
#eval evalM safeDivExc (.add (.num 4) (.div (.num 6) (.num 0)))

Logging computations - an example of the writer monad
Let's look at a more advanced example: an evaluator that also logs the
computation it executes in a linear log of strings. The challenge here is that
we still have to combine that with Option to support the divide-by-zero
case, so we'll start by creating a new structure to carry the state of the
computation:
structure LoggedOption (α : Type) where
  value : Option α
  log : List String

This will be the result of one eval call; it produces an optional value,
along with a list of strings (the log). Here's the Monad implementation for
this type:
instance : Monad LoggedOption where
  pure x := ⟨some x, []⟩
  bind v next :=
    match v.value with
    | none => ⟨none, v.log⟩
    | some x =>
      let nextResult := next x
      ⟨nextResult.value, v.log ++ nextResult.log⟩

The main idea is combining the stored log with the log of the next computation
by appending them (thus accumulating a linear log). Here's our evaluator:
def evalLogged : Expr → LoggedOption Int
  | .num n => pure n
  | .add a b => do
    let x ← evalLogged a
    let y ← evalLogged b
    ⟨some (x + y), [s!"adding {x} and {y}"]⟩
  | .div a b => do
    let x ← evalLogged a
    let y ← evalLogged b
    match y with
    | 0 => ⟨none, [s!"dividing {x} by zero"]⟩
    | _ => ⟨some (x / y), [s!"dividing {x} by {y}"]⟩

Note how the code of evalLogged doesn't have to deal with the mechanics
of logging too much (other than adding new log entries). All of that is hidden
within the monad instance. LoggedOption is an example of the writer monad,
which is a write-only version of the state monad.
State monad
One of the most important use cases of monads in functional programming
languages is modeling mutable state through a computation.
A stateful computation is modeled as a function that takes an initial state
and returns a tuple containing the result value and a new, updated state. In
Lean notation:
def State (σ : Type) (α : Type) : Type :=
  σ → (α × σ)

To demonstrate this in action, let's enhance our evaluator to support variable
assignments and lookups. Our state is going to be an association list of
name, value pairs:
abbrev Vars := List (String × Int)

And we'll augment our expression enum with additional operations:
inductive ExprV where
  | num : Int → ExprV
  | add : ExprV → ExprV → ExprV
  | div : ExprV → ExprV → ExprV
  | store : String → ExprV → ExprV
  | load : String → ExprV

This is going to be our state monad:
structure EvalM (α : Type) where
  run : Vars → Option (α × Vars)

Note the correspondence of the run function to the State signature
above:
It takes the current state, which for our use cases is an association list
carrying values for all defined variables.
It returns an optional result which is a pair of some value (in our case,
the result of the computation) and an updated state.
This is its Monad class implementation:
instance : Monad EvalM where
  pure x := ⟨fun vars => some (x, vars)⟩
  bind action next := ⟨fun vars =>
    match action.run vars with
    | none => none
    | some (x, vars') => (next x).run vars'⟩

And finally, the evaluator:
def evalState : ExprV → EvalM Int
  | .num n => pure n
  | .add a b => do
    let x ← evalState a
    let y ← evalState b
    pure (x + y)
  | .div a b => do
    let x ← evalState a
    let y ← evalState b
    ⟨fun vars => (safeDiv x y).map (fun value => (value, vars))⟩
  | .load name =>
    ⟨fun vars => do
      let value ← vars.lookup name
      pure (value, vars)⟩
  | .store name rhs => do
    let value ← evalState rhs
    ⟨fun vars =>
      let vars' := (name, value) :: vars.filter (fun p => p.1 != name)
      some (value, vars')⟩

Operations that don't deal with variables directly (like .num and
.add) just do their work as before. .div only has to deal with the
actual monad type to ensure that none is propagated in case of division
by zero. Note also that this evaluator supports stores as expressions, since
they separately return a value and the updated state; therefore, computations
like this one will work:
-- (x := 12) + (x / 3): the right operand sees the left operand's assignment.
#eval (evalState
  (.add (.store "x" (.num 12))
        (.div (.load "x") (.num 3)))).run []

Producing the result some (16, [("x", 12)]).
In a language with mutable state, modeling side effects is easy - just assign
some state (like a struct field or class member). In a functional language like
Lean, however, we have to carry this state across the computations explicitly;
monads help us do this with elegance - by hiding most of the mechanics of
actually carrying the state around, the majority of the code remains free
of bookkeeping.
IO monad
Perhaps the most well known example of a monad in functional programming
languages like Lean and Haskell is IO. To anyone who's written a "real"
program that interacts with the outer world, IO is very familiar. Here's
a customized "Hello" program that's typically taught in the first 15
minutes of learning a new programming language:
def greet : IO Unit := do
  let stdin ← IO.getStdin
  IO.println "What is your name?"
  let name ← stdin.getLine
  IO.println s!"Hello, {name}"

Note the do notation here, suggesting monads. As mentioned before, do
is syntactic sugar for the monad's bind method, or the >>= operator; we
can rewrite this code more explicitly as:
def greetBind : IO Unit :=
  IO.getStdin >>= fun stdin =>
  IO.println "What is your name?" >>= fun _ =>
  stdin.getLine >>= fun name =>
  IO.println s!"Hello, {name}"

In essence, IO is a state monad, where the state carried around represents
the "outside world". IO operations like println act on that world,
and its state is carried over using bind, like other state monads.
Here's a version of our expression evaluator that logs directly to standard out,
instead of collecting the log as a list of strings:
def evalIO : Expr → OptionT IO Int
  | .num n => pure n
  | .add a b => do
    let x ← evalIO a
    let y ← evalIO b
    IO.println s!"adding {x} and {y}"
    pure (x + y)
  | .div a b => do
    let x ← evalIO a
    let y ← evalIO b
    IO.println s!"dividing {x} by {y}"
    OptionT.mk (pure (safeDiv x y))

The only unusual construct here is OptionT, which is a monad transformer
that helps us compose Option (for propagating failure from safe division)
with the IO Monad [4].
The IO monad also supports throw for Python-like exception behavior,
but in this example we use Option explicitly; exceptions are a matter of
programming preference, and using them inside library functions like eval
doesn't feel right to me.
Monad laws in Lean
Just like in Haskell, monads in Lean should obey certain laws.
Those are:
Left identity: wrapping a value in pure and immediately passing it to
f with bind should be equivalent to just calling f on the value:
pure v >>= f       =    f v

Right identity: extracting a value from a computation and immediately
wrapping it with pure again should not change the computation:
m >>= pure         =    m

Associativity: the grouping of operations doesn't matter, as long as their
order remains the same:
(m >>= f) >>= g    =    m >>= (fun v => f v >>= g)

Let's see how Option obeys these laws.
For left identity, pure v is some v and the bind implementation
matches some x to next x, which is equivalent to f v.
For right identity, m >>= pure just rewraps a some value in pure,
leaving none alone - this is equivalent to keeping things as they are.
For associativity, if m is none then both sides are none. If m
is some v, the left side is f v >>= g, and the right side reduces to
the same, so again they are equivalent.
While Lean doesn't enforce that a Monad instance obeys these laws, it has
a separate type class called LawfulMonad which does require Lean proofs;
this is useful for Lean's main use case - proving theorems about programs,
expressed through its powerful type system. But this is a topic for another
day.


[1]We've replaced some n by pure n in the .num case; technically
this isn't necessary, but it will be useful later in the post when we
examine other types implementing Monad.


[2]This is explored in Philip Wadler's classical paper "The essence of
functional programming".


[3]Except also happens to implement Monad.


[4]We could also have used OptionT in earlier examples, e.g. instead
of explicitly defining LoggedOption - try changing that code to use
OptionT as an exercise.
